vignette:
He is nineteen, European, and works as a counselor at a youth activity center, a job people often praise him for being “naturally good at.” He knows how to sit still while someone else talks. He knows how to ask careful questions and keep his face soft. What people do not see is how much effort it takes now to stay present when anyone mentions hospitals, blood tests, or the word “scan.” He is in a relationship with his girlfriend, who says he seems older than his age in some ways and much younger in others. She means that he can listen to another person’s pain for an hour and then panic if she does not text back for twenty minutes.

The story begins just over a year ago, when what seemed like an ordinary illness stopped feeling ordinary. At first he tries to explain it away: the fatigue, the fevers, the bruises that appear without him remembering any impact. He is still going to work then, sitting with teenagers after school, telling them to drink water, sleep more, talk to someone if they are overwhelmed. He says these things while feeling a strange heaviness in his own body, as if he is moving through wet concrete. When he nearly faints one afternoon, a colleague insists he go to hospital.

He remembers the emergency department in fragments that have never properly joined together. The bright strip lighting. The smell of antiseptic. A nurse repeating his name. His mother arriving with her coat half-buttoned. Then the doctor’s face, too serious too quickly. He has an aggressive blood disorder, they tell him, and they need to act fast. He does not remember the exact wording anymore, only the feeling that the room narrows and sound becomes far away. In the days that follow, there are more tests, consent forms, lines inserted into his arm, bags of fluid dripping beside him through the night. He becomes preoccupied with numbers—heart rate, white cell count, oxygen saturation—as though watching them closely might keep him alive.

During the worst stretch of the illness, he is convinced he may die. He does not say this aloud often because everyone around him is trying to sound hopeful, but at night he stares at the monitor and imagines his girlfriend receiving a phone call. He notices every sensation in his body and interprets it as danger: a skipped beat, a pressure in his chest, a wave of nausea. Once, when an alarm goes off in another patient’s bay, he starts shaking so hard he cannot hold the cup of water someone gives him. Even after his condition stabilizes, his body does not seem to understand that the immediate threat has passed.

He returns home thinner, weaker, and full of restless energy that does not feel like relief. Sleep becomes the first thing he loses. He lies in bed replaying small moments from the hospital with sharp, unwanted clarity: the doctor saying “serious,” the sound of trolley wheels at night, his mother crying in the corridor when she thought he could not hear. Sometimes he wakes drenched in sweat after dreams in which he is trying to call for help and no sound comes out. On those mornings he checks his breathing before he gets out of bed and presses his fingers to his neck to make sure his pulse is still there.

Back at work, he finds himself reacting to things that never used to matter. If a young person mentions a parent on a cancer ward, his stomach drops. If someone looks pale, he has to stop himself from urging them to go straight to A&E. He keeps a steady voice, but inside he is elsewhere—back under fluorescent lights, waiting for someone to tell him whether he will live. He starts avoiding certain cases, then certain corridors in the health center attached to his workplace. He tells colleagues he is busy with paperwork. He begins arriving late because he circles the block when he sees an ambulance parked outside.

His girlfriend notices that he startles violently now. The beep of the microwave, a late-night phone call, even the vibration of his own mobile on the table can make him jump and swear. He becomes irritable in ways that embarrass him. When she asks how he is feeling after a follow-up appointment, he snaps that he is “fine,” then spends the rest of the evening ashamed and withdrawn. He no longer trusts his body, and that mistrust leaks into everything. If she wants to make plans for the summer, he hesitates, as though committing to the future might tempt fate.

He tells other people he is lucky, because he survived, because the doctors caught it, because things could have been worse. He believes all of that and still feels trapped by what happened. He checks his temperature repeatedly when he feels warm. He googles symptoms he already knows too much about. In crowded places he silently identifies exits and wonders how long it would take for paramedics to arrive. Some part of him remains in that hospital bed, waiting for the next bad news.

What troubles him most is that he cannot counsel himself out of it. He can hear the reassurance in his own thoughts and not believe it. He can tell a frightened teenager that the danger is over while his own heart is pounding as if it is happening again. In the present, his life looks as though it is back on track: he is working, still with his girlfriend, making jokes, showing up. But much of each day is organized around not feeling that old fear too fully, because when it breaks through, he is nineteen again and certain he might not survive the night.
